mainTopic: Skills of a תלמיד חכם; the trained שוחט and checking the סימנים; רב הונא's presumption of permission after שחיטה
overview: The amud opens by finishing a point about forbidden fat: the membrane on top does not protect the meat, because the שוחט's hand rubs it until it falls apart. רב teaches that a תלמיד חכם must learn writing, שחיטה and מילה, and another version adds the תפילין knot, ברכת חתנים and ציצית. שמואל rules that we may not eat from a טבח who does not know the five הלכות שחיטה, even if he slaughtered well in front of us a few times, because he may make a mistake without realizing it. שמואל also says the טבח must check the סימנים after slaughtering. רב יוסף's proof for this from רבי שמעון is turned aside. If the טבח did not check, one view says the animal is a טרפה and the ברייתא says it is a נבלה. The גמרא explains that both views build on רב הונא's rule: a living animal is presumed forbidden until we know it was slaughtered properly, and after that it is presumed permitted even if a flaw shows up. רב הונא rules that when a wolf returns the innards with holes, we do not worry that it bit right where an earlier hole was. רבי אבא then starts to challenge him from a case of a bird pecking a fig, and that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Isn't there also a membrane on top?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a membrane (קרמא) protects the meat when the fat is below, there should also be a membrane on top that protects it.
steps.simpleTranslation: From above there is also a membrane, isn't there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing the earlier discussion about forbidden fat touching meat. It challenges the idea that only the membrane underneath protects the meat, since the fat has a membrane on top too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier reasoning relied on a membrane blocking the fat from flowing into the meat. The challenge is that the same kind of membrane exists on the upper side. So why should the position of the fat make any difference?

keyTerms.meaning: A thin membrane or skin covering the fat

phrases.english: From above, too, there is a membrane?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning from the previous section of the daf about the membrane under the fat.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the membrane protects the meat only in one position
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a membrane blocks the fat from below, a membrane on top should block it just as well.

steps.title: The slaughterer's hand breaks up the upper membrane
steps.stepSummary: The upper membrane does not protect, because the טבח's hand keeps touching it and it falls apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the hand of the slaughterer handles it, it crumbles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The upper membrane gets rubbed by the slaughterer's hand while he works, so it breaks apart and no longer blocks the fat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides have a membrane, but they are not in the same condition. The bottom one stays whole. The top one is damaged by handling, so it cannot stop the fat from flowing onto the meat.

phrases.english: Since the hand of the slaughterer handles it, it crumbles.
phrases.notes: The "it" is the upper membrane. Once it is broken, the fat can flow onto the meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual distinction between the two membranes
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The upper membrane should protect the meat just like the lower one does.
steps.terutzMaskana: The upper membrane is ruined by the slaughterer's handling, so only the lower one protects.

steps.title: Three skills a Torah scholar must learn
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב teaches that a תלמיד חכם must learn three practical skills: writing, שחיטה, and מילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A Torah scholar needs to learn three things: writing, slaughtering, and circumcision.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic, linked to the previous one because it involves שחיטה. רב says a תלמיד חכם must know three hands-on skills.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are skills that come up in Jewish life where someone needs to be able to do the job properly. A תלמיד חכם should be able to do them himself and not only know the theory.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמִיד חָכָם צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּלְמוֹד שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים:
phrases.english: A Torah scholar needs to learn three things:
Writing, slaughtering, and circumcision.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New teaching, linked by the theme of שחיטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם must learn writing, שחיטה, and מילה.

steps.title: Three more skills in another version of רב
steps.stepSummary: רב חנניה בר שלמיא, also quoting רב, adds three more skills: tying the knot of תפילין, saying ברכת חתנים, and making ציצית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חנניה בר שלמיא said in the name of רב: Also the knot of תפילין, the blessing of the grooms, and ציצית.
steps.whatsHappening: A second student reports רב's teaching with a longer list. He keeps the first three and adds three more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אף ("also") shows he is adding to the first list, not replacing it. Now we have two versions of what רב said, and the גמרא will next explain the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: The special knot of the תפילין straps
The blessings said for a bride and groom (שבע ברכות)
Ritual fringes on a four-cornered garment

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חֲנַנְיָא בַּר שֶׁלֶמְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אָמַר:
phrases.english: And Rav Ḥananya bar Shelamya said in the name of Rav:
Also the knot of the phylacteries,
phrases.notes: He means a scholar must also know how to tie it himself.

phrases.english: and the blessing of the grooms, and ritual fringes.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב חֲנַנְיָא בַּר שֶׁלֶמְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of רב's teaching that adds to the list in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם must also learn the תפילין knot, ברכת חתנים, and ציצית.

steps.title: Why the first version leaves these out
steps.stepSummary: The other version (רב יהודה) does not list the extra three because they are common skills that everyone knows.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one: these are common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב יהודה's version did not include the extra three skills. They are so common that a scholar will know them anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions do not really disagree about whether these skills matter. The first version just did not need to mention them, since people learn them without special training.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree a scholar should know all six skills. רב יהודה's version lists only the three that need special training.

phrases.english: And the other one: these are common.
phrases.notes: "The other one" is רב יהודה's version. The hidden question is why he left out the extra three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the gap between the versions in steps 3 and 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining why something was left out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יהודה's version might seem to hold that a scholar does not need these three skills.
steps.terutzMaskana: He left them out only because they are common and need no special learning.

steps.title: A slaughterer who doesn't know the laws
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל: it is forbidden to eat from a טבח who does not know הלכות שחיטה. These laws are the five things that make a שחיטה invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Any slaughterer who does not know the laws of slaughter, it is forbidden to eat from his slaughter. These are the laws of slaughter: pausing, pressing, covering, slipping out of place, and tearing out.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching. שמואל rules that we may not eat meat slaughtered by someone who has not learned the laws of שחיטה, and he lists the five main laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The five laws (שהייה, דרסה, חלדה, הגרמה, עיקור) are the five mistakes that make a שחיטה invalid. שמואל says what matters is not only doing the cut, but knowing these rules.

keyTerms.meaning: Pausing in the middle of the cut
Pressing the knife down instead of drawing it back and forth
Hiding the knife under the windpipe or food pipe while cutting
Slipping the cut outside the proper area of the neck
Tearing the pipes out of place before cutting them

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule for kosher meat: a שוחט must be properly trained, not just skilled with a knife.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל טַבָּח שֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ הִלְכוֹת שְׁחִיטָה
phrases.english: Any slaughterer who does not know the laws of slaughter,
it is forbidden to eat from his slaughter.
And these are the laws of slaughter:
Pausing, pressing, covering, slipping out of place, and tearing out.
phrases.notes: These are the five mistakes that make a שחיטה invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New teaching on the theme of שחיטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat from a טבח who does not know the five הלכות שחיטה is forbidden.

steps.title: Why say this? We already learned all these laws
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what שמואל adds, since all five laws are already taught in the משניות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned all of them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's teaching as unnecessary. The five laws already appear in the משניות, so it seems obvious that someone who doesn't know them is not fit to slaughter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is not against the rule itself but against the need to state it. If the משנה already says these mistakes make a שחיטה invalid, then of course a slaughterer must know them.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (What is new here?)
We have learned all of them (in the משנה)

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We learned all of them!
phrases.notes: All five laws are already taught in the משניות of this מסכת.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן כּוּלְּהוּ תְּנִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether שמואל's teaching in step 6 adds anything.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the משנה already teaches the five laws, it is obvious that a slaughterer must know them.

steps.title: Even a good track record is not enough
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's point is needed for a slaughterer who has already slaughtered well in front of us two or three times. We still may not rely on him, because without learning he might pause or press and not know it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where he slaughtered in front of us two or three times and did it well. You might have said: since he did the others well, this one is also fine. So he teaches us: since he did not learn, sometimes he pauses or presses and doesn't even know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שמואל is teaching something new. Even if an untrained slaughterer did good work in front of us several times, we cannot trust his other slaughterings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without שמואל, we might have assumed his good record proves he is reliable. שמואל teaches that someone who never learned the laws can make a mistake like שהייה or דרסה without realizing it. So he will not stop or tell us, and seeing good results a few times is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case
You might have said (the mistaken assumption)

steps.whatToRemember: A slaughterer must actually learn הלכות שחיטה. A good track record is not enough, because an untrained person can make a mistake and not know it.
steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not that he is dishonest. He simply cannot recognize his own mistakes, because he never learned what counts as a mistake.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the reason a שוחט must be trained and checked, not just watched a few times.

phrases.aramaic: לָא צְרִיכָא, שֶׁשָּׁחַט לְפָנֵינוּ שְׁתַּיִם וְשָׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים
phrases.english: No, it is needed where he slaughtered before us two and three times
and slaughtered well;
you might have said: since the other ones he slaughtered well,
this one too he slaughtered well,
phrases.notes: "This one" means an animal he slaughtered when we were not watching.

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: כֵּיוָן דְּלָא גְּמִר,
phrases.english: so he teaches us: since he did not learn,
sometimes he pauses and presses and does not know.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא שֶׁשָּׁחַט לְפָנֵינוּ שְׁתַּיִם וְשָׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7 by pointing to a case where שמואל's teaching is new.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the teaching to a specific case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A slaughterer who did well before us two or three times could be trusted even without learning.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without learning, he may make a mistake and not know it, so his slaughter is forbidden.

steps.title: The slaughterer must check the סימנים after slaughtering
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל: after שחיטה, the טבח must check the סימנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The slaughterer must check the סימנים after the slaughter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from שמואל. After he slaughters, the טבח has to look at the סימנים to make sure they were cut properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last steps were about what the טבח must know before he slaughters. This rule adds a duty after the slaughter: he must actually look and check that the cut was done right.

keyTerms.meaning: The two pipes cut in שחיטה: the windpipe (קנה) and the food pipe (ושט)

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
The slaughterer must check the simanim
after the slaughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second rule of רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, following the rule about a טבח who doesn't know the laws.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A טבח must check the סימנים after slaughtering.

steps.title: רב יוסף brings support from רבי שמעון's pause rule
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says a משנה already shows this: רבי שמעון measures a disqualifying pause by the time it takes to do a 'checking', which must be the checking of the סימנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: We also learned this in a משנה. רבי שמעון says: If he paused for the length of a checking, the שחיטה is invalid. Doesn't this mean the time it takes to check the סימנים?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף tries to prove שמואל's rule from a משנה. רבי שמעון measures a pause by the length of 'a checking', and רב יוסף reads that as checking the סימנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה uses 'checking the סימנים' as a standard measure of time, then such checking must be a normal, required step. That would support שמואל's rule that a טבח must check them.

keyTerms.meaning: Paused or delayed in the middle of the שחיטה, one of the five things that invalidate it
The amount of time it takes to do a checking
Isn't it…? A way of offering a proof

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
We too have learned this in a mishna:
Rabbi Shimon says:
If he paused for the length of a checking, [the slaughter is invalid].
Is it not the length of time it takes to check the simanim?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a proof from a משנה for שמואל's rule.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's rule that the סימנים must be checked after שחיטה
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי שמעון in a משנה, who measures a pause by the length of a 'checking'

steps.title: אביי: the checking means checking by a scholar
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects the proof. רבי יוחנן explained the 'checking' as the time of a checking by a חכם, meaning checking the knife.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: No. This is what רבי יוחנן said: It means the length of time of a checking by a חכם.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes away רב יוסף's proof. He says the 'checking' in the משנה is not checking the סימנים but a checking done by a חכם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the 'checking' is the knife being checked by a חכם, the משנה says nothing about checking the סימנים. So the proof for שמואל falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: A checking done by a Torah scholar, here the checking of the knife
This is what he said, the correct way to read it

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: No,
this is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
the length of a checking by a scholar.
phrases.notes: He means the time it takes to bring the knife to a חכם to be checked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 10 by reading the משנה differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the משנה, not שמואל's rule itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The 'checking' in the משנה refers to a checking by a חכם, not to checking the סימנים.

steps.title: Objection: that measure would keep changing
steps.stepSummary: If the measure is the time of bringing the knife to a חכם, the amount of time would change from case to case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, you have made your rule depend on changing measures!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges אביי's reading. A measure that depends on going to a חכם is not a fixed amount of time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes the חכם is close by and sometimes far away. A rule about how long a pause can be needs one fixed length, so this reading seems to fail.

keyTerms.meaning: You have made your words depend on changing amounts, so there is no fixed measure

phrases.english: If so,
you have given your words over to changing measures!
phrases.notes: The time would depend on how far away the חכם happens to be.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's reading in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading 'כדי ביקור' as a checking by a חכם
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A time measure has to be fixed, but the time it takes to reach a חכם changes with distance.

steps.title: The time it takes a scholarly slaughterer to check
steps.stepSummary: The measure is the time a טבח who is himself a חכם takes to check the knife.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means the length of time a slaughterer who is a חכם takes to do the checking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading. The checking is done by the טבח himself, who is a חכם, so no travel time is counted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the חכם is the טבח himself, the only time counted is the checking itself. That is a steady, fixed amount, which answers the objection. The משנה still does not prove שמואל's rule about checking the סימנים.

keyTerms.meaning: A slaughterer who is himself a Torah scholar

phrases.english: Rather, the length of a checking by a slaughterer who is a scholar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 12 by adjusting אביי's reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Refining the definition of the measure
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The measure includes going to a חכם, so it would change from case to case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The measure is the time a טבח who is a חכם takes to check, which is a fixed amount.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the attempted proof. שמואל's rule stands on its own and is not shown by this משנה.

steps.title: What if he did not check?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is if the טבח did not check the סימנים after slaughtering.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not check, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to שמואל's rule and asks what happens to the animal when the טבח skipped the check.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said the טבח must check. Now the question is whether skipping the check affects the animal's status, and if so, how badly.

phrases.english: If he did not check, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to שמואל's rule from step 9 to ask about a טבח who did not check.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The status of an animal whose סימנים were not checked after שחיטה.

steps.title: First view: it is a טרפה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן אנטיגנוס in the name of רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי: the animal is a טרפה and may not be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן אנטיגנוס said in the name of רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי: It is a טרפה, and it is forbidden to eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer: if he didn't check, the animal is treated as a טרפה, so you may not eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A טרפה is forbidden to eat, but it does not make things impure the way a נבלה does. So this view forbids eating the animal but does not give it טומאה. Step 19 explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: A slaughtered animal that is forbidden to eat, but does not give impurity

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמַר:
phrases.english: said in the name of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yannai:
It is a treifa, and it is forbidden to eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן אַנְטִיגְנוֹס מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The unchecked animal is a טרפה: forbidden to eat, but it does not give impurity.

steps.title: A ברייתא: it is a נבלה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the unchecked animal is a נבלה and makes a person impure by carrying it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: It is a נבלה, and it makes a person impure through carrying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, stricter view from a ברייתא. The unchecked animal counts as a נבלה, an animal that was never properly slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נבלה is not just forbidden to eat. It also gives טומאה to someone who carries it. So this view treats the animal as if no valid שחיטה happened at all.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that died without a valid שחיטה
Makes a person impure when he carries it
A ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up טרפה and נבלה. Both are forbidden to eat, but only a נבלה makes someone impure. That difference is the whole argument here.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:
It is a neveila, and it makes impure through carrying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, stricter answer that disagrees with step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unchecked animal is a נבלה and gives impurity by carrying.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle the two views disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It wants to find the deeper idea behind the טרפה view and the נבלה view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both views agree you may not eat the animal. The question is why one says it is only a טרפה while the other says it is a full נבלה.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the argument between steps 15 and 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The principle behind the טרפה versus נבלה disagreement.

steps.title: They argue about רב הונא's rule of presumed status
steps.stepSummary: The argument depends on רב הונא: a living animal is presumed forbidden until we know it was slaughtered properly; once slaughtered, it is presumed permitted until we know it became a טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about רב הונא's rule. He said: A living animal is presumed forbidden until you know how it was slaughtered. Once it is slaughtered, it is presumed permitted until you know how it became a טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the argument connects to רב הונא's rule about an animal's חזקה (presumed status). The גמרא will next show how each view fits with this rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא gives two stages. Before a known proper שחיטה, the animal keeps its forbidden status. After a proper שחיטה, it keeps a permitted status unless we learn of a problem. An unchecked animal sits right between these stages, which is why the two views can disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Presumed to be forbidden until shown otherwise
Presumed to be permitted until shown otherwise
An animal while it is still alive

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's two-stage rule: alive means presumed forbidden until a proper שחיטה is known; slaughtered means presumed permitted until a טרפה problem is known.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב הונא's rule of חזקה is a key principle in the laws of שחיטה and comes up often when there is a doubt about an animal.

phrases.english: About the teaching of Rav Huna, who said:
An animal in its lifetime
stands in a presumed status of forbidden,
until it becomes known to you how it was slaughtered.
Once it was slaughtered, it is in a presumed status of permitted,
until it becomes known to you how it became a treifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17 by naming the principle behind the argument.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The disagreement depends on רב הונא's rule of presumed status before and after שחיטה.

steps.title: Both sides use the presumption of prohibition differently
steps.stepSummary: Both views agree a living animal starts out forbidden. The ברייתא also treats it as a dead carcass that makes a person impure. רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי applies the presumption only to eating, not to impurity.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds: the animal stays in its presumption of prohibition, and now it is dead, so it is a נבלה. The other Sage holds: we apply the presumption of prohibition, but we do not apply a presumption of impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer from step 18. It shows exactly how each side uses רב הונא's rule about a living animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since nobody checked the סימנים, the animal never left its starting status of 'forbidden.' The ברייתא goes all the way: an animal not known to be slaughtered properly counts as one that simply died, which is a נבלה and makes a person impure. רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי says the starting status was only 'forbidden to eat.' A living animal was never impure, so there is no starting impurity to carry over, and the animal is only a טרפה.

keyTerms.meaning: Presumption of prohibition: the status of being forbidden until we know otherwise
An animal that died without a proper שחיטה; it makes a person impure

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי says the animal is permitted. Both sides forbid eating it. The only argument is whether it also makes a person impure.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that an unchecked animal may not be eaten. The ברייתא adds that it is a נבלה and makes a person impure. רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי says it is only a טרפה, because a living animal never had a status of impurity.

phrases.english: One Sage holds: it stands in a presumption of prohibition,
phrases.notes: This first Sage is the ברייתא, which said the animal is a נבלה.

phrases.english: and now it is dead;
phrases.notes: 'Dead' here means it counts as an animal that died without שחיטה, which is a נבלה.

phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: a presumption of prohibition we do say,
a presumption of impurity we do not say.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in step 18 by applying רב הונא's rule to each side of the dispute.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא carries the presumption of prohibition all the way to נבלה status. רבי אלעזר ברבי ינאי limits it to the prohibition of eating, with no impurity.

steps.title: רב הונא's rule examined on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to רב הונא's statement to study it directly. A living animal is forbidden until we know it was slaughtered properly. Once slaughtered, it is permitted until we know it became a טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: רב הונא said: An animal in its lifetime stands as forbidden until you know how it was slaughtered. Once slaughtered, it stands as permitted until you know how it became a טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks closely at רב הונא's statement by itself. This sets up a question about his exact wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, רב הונא's rule was only a tool for explaining the dispute. Now it becomes the topic itself. The rule has two stages: before שחיטה the default is 'forbidden,' and after a proper שחיטה the default flips to 'permitted.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': the גמרא turns back to study a statement it quoted earlier
An animal with a fatal defect; forbidden to eat even after שחיטה

phrases.english: The matter itself:
phrases.notes: The גמרא goes back to look at רב הונא's statement from step 18 on its own.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
An animal in its lifetime stands in a presumption of prohibition
until it becomes known to you how it was slaughtered;
once slaughtered, it stands in a presumption of permission
until it becomes known to you how it became a tereifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the dispute behind and opens a new discussion of רב הונא's statement itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A living animal is presumed forbidden until we know it was properly slaughtered. After שחיטה it is presumed permitted until we know it became a טרפה.

steps.title: Why not just say it became permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's wording. Why speak of a 'presumption of permission'? He could simply say that once slaughtered, the animal is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'Once slaughtered, it became permitted'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב הונא's choice of words. It suggests a simpler phrasing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'presumption' (חזקה) sounds like a status that could be questioned. After a proper שחיטה, why do we need a presumption at all? The animal should just be permitted. The challenge pushes רב הונא's wording to show it is teaching something extra.

keyTerms.meaning: And let him say: a challenge suggesting better wording

phrases.english: Let him say: 'Once slaughtered, it became permitted'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רב הונא's statement from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's phrase 'stands in a presumption of permission'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: After proper שחיטה the animal is simply permitted, so the word 'presumption' seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The presumption holds even when a flaw shows up
steps.stepSummary: The wording teaches that even if a possible defect later appears in the slaughtered animal, it keeps its presumption of permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us that even though a flaw arose in it, it stays permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב הונא's word 'presumption' is deliberate. It teaches a new point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'it became permitted' would cover only a normal, clean case. By calling it a 'presumption,' רב הונא tells us the permitted status is strong enough to survive doubt. Even if some damage shows up after שחיטה, we assume it happened after the שחיטה and not before.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
A flaw or defect that raises doubt

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: damage found after שחיטה does not, by itself, make the animal forbidden. The next question tests exactly this point.

phrases.english: This teaches us,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּאִיתְיְלִיד בַּהּ רֵיעוּתָא.
phrases.english: that even though a flaw arose in it, it still keeps its status.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the wording is deliberate and teaches a new point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Presumption' seems like extra wording; 'became permitted' would be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Presumption' teaches that the permitted status survives even when a flaw appears after שחיטה.

steps.title: רבי אבא asks about a wolf and the innards
steps.stepSummary: As an example of a flaw arising after שחיטה, the גמרא brings רבי אבא's question to רב הונא. What if a wolf came and took the innards of a slaughtered animal?
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אבא asked רב הונא: a wolf came and took the innards; what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real case that fits the 'flaw' רב הונא was talking about. It begins with רבי אבא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'as' links this question to the point just made. A wolf damaging a slaughtered animal is the kind of flaw that could raise doubt. The question asks whether the presumption of permission still holds in such a case.

keyTerms.meaning: Asked of him: a question put to a teacher

phrases.aramaic: כְּדִבְעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא מֵרַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Abba asked of Rav Huna:

phrases.aramaic: בָּא זְאֵב וְנָטַל בְּנֵי מֵעַיִם, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: A wolf came and took the innards; what is the law?
phrases.notes: This is an animal that was already slaughtered. A hole in the innards is a sign of a טרפה.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדִבְעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא מֵרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a case that fits the 'flaw after שחיטה' idea from step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a slaughtered animal stays permitted after a wolf took its innards.

steps.title: If the innards are gone, there is nothing to ask
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the first version of the question. If the wolf took the innards away, they are not here, so there is no flaw to see.
steps.simpleTranslation: Took?! But they are not here!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on how the question was worded. It says the case as stated raises no doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the innards are simply gone, we see no hole and no sign of a טרפה. With no sign of a problem, the animal stays in its presumption of permission. So the question needs to be reworded.

phrases.english: Took?! But they are not here,
phrases.notes: With the innards gone, there is no sign of any flaw to worry about.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רבי אבא's question in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of a wolf that took the innards
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the innards are gone, there is no visible flaw. So the animal simply stays permitted, and there is no question.

steps.title: Rewording: the wolf punctured the innards
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rewords the question. Maybe it means the wolf punctured the innards; what is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it punctured the innards; what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new version of רבי אבא's question so that there is a real doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is a visible hole in the innards, which is a sign of a טרפה. This seems to make the question work. But the next step will challenge this version too.

phrases.english: Rather, it punctured the innards; what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to step 24 by rewording the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewords the case of the question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about a wolf taking the innards away.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about a wolf puncturing the innards.

steps.title: We saw the wolf make the holes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects again. If the wolf punctured them in front of us, we know the holes came from the wolf after שחיטה. So there is still no doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Punctured?! But we see that it was the wolf that punctured them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second version of the question as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we watched the wolf make the holes, they clearly came after the שחיטה. A hole made after שחיטה does not make the animal a טרפה. So this version also has no real doubt.

phrases.aramaic: נָקַב?! הָא קָא חָזֵינַן דְּהוּא נַקְבִינְהוּ!
phrases.english: Punctured?! But we see that it punctured them!

steps.triggerLanguage: נָקַב?! הָא קָא חָזֵינַן דְּהוּא נַקְבִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rewording offered in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of a wolf puncturing the innards
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: We saw the wolf make the holes after שחיטה, so the animal was not a טרפה. There is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The real question: the wolf returned them with holes
steps.stepSummary: The final version: the wolf took the innards away and brought them back with holes. Do we worry that one of the wolf's holes is right where an earlier hole already was, which would make the animal a טרפה?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the wolf took them and returned them punctured; what is the law? Do we worry that maybe it punctured right where a hole already was, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the true form of רבי אבא's question. It spells out the exact doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here we did not see when the holes were made. The wolf may have bitten exactly where a hole from before the שחיטה already existed, hiding a real טרפה. The question is whether that worry beats the presumption of permission that רב הונא taught.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned; we worry about the possibility
In the place of an existing hole

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אבא's real question: a wolf took the innards and returned them with holes. Do we fear the holes hide an earlier hole from before the שחיטה, or does the presumption of permission win?
steps.whyThisMatters: This case tests how strong רב הונא's presumption of permission is when a flaw appears after שחיטה and its timing is unclear.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא נְטָלָן וְהֶחְזִירָן כְּשֶׁהֵן נְקוּבִין, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: Rather, it took them and returned them when they are punctured; what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא בִּמְקוֹם נֶקֶב נָקַב,
phrases.english: Are we concerned that perhaps it punctured in the place of a hole,
phrases.notes: He means a hole that was already there before the שחיטה, which would have made the animal a טרפה from the start.

phrases.english: or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא נְטָלָן וְהֶחְזִירָן כְּשֶׁהֵן נְקוּבִין, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to step 26 with the final, precise version of the question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewords the case so that there is a real doubt
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about a wolf puncturing the innards in front of us.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about innards taken away and returned with holes, where an earlier hole could be hidden.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether we worry that the wolf's holes hide a hole from before the שחיטה.

steps.title: רב הונא: we do not worry about a hole on top of a hole
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that we do not worry that the wolf's bite landed exactly on an earlier hole. So the animal stays kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We do not worry that maybe the wolf made its hole in the same place where there was already a hole.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives his answer to the wolf question from Step 27. We do not worry, so the animal is not treated as a טרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The holes we see can be explained by the wolf, and those holes came after שחיטה, so they do not matter. The only problem would be if one wolf bite hid an older hole from before שחיטה. רב הונא says we do not assume that unlikely overlap, so the animal keeps its kosher status.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not worry; we do not take this possibility into account
A hole or puncture in an organ, which can make an animal a טרפה

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's rule: when the wolf brings back punctured innards, we do not suspect that a bite landed on an earlier hole. The animal is kosher.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main ruling the next steps will test. רבי אבא is about to challenge it.

phrases.english: He said to him: We are not concerned
phrases.notes: "He" is רב הונא, answering רבי אבא's question about the wolf.

phrases.english: that perhaps it punctured in the place of a hole.
phrases.notes: He means the wolf's bite landing exactly on a hole that was already there before שחיטה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the final version of רבי אבא's question from Step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do we worry that the wolf's hole is exactly where an earlier hole already was?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. We do not worry about this, so the animal is kosher.

steps.title: רבי אבא begins an objection: the bird and the mouse
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא starts to challenge רב הונא by quoting a case. Someone saw a bird pecking at a fig or a mouse gnawing at melons.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised an objection to him: If someone saw a bird pecking at a fig, or a mouse gnawing at melons...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא begins to challenge רב הונא's ruling by quoting a case. This step only sets up the case; the ruling that makes up the challenge comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setup is like the wolf case: we see marks on food, and they could come from the animal we saw. The case may also allow for an earlier hole hidden under those marks. רבי אבא will use the ruling of this case to argue that we do worry about a hole on top of a hole.

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him: If one saw a bird
phrases.notes: Now רבי אבא is challenging רב הונא's answer.

phrases.english: pecking at a fig
or a mouse gnawing at melons,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a challenge against רב הונא's ruling in Step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that we do not worry the wolf bit exactly where an earlier hole was.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A similar case of holes in food made by a bird or mouse will be quoted. Its ruling will suggest that we do worry about a hidden earlier hole.
